name: Soldier Field
body: NASCAR once paved a half-mile oval inside a football stadium and ran a points race on it. Soldier Field, July 1956, 14,402 people on the Chicago lakefront watching Fireball Roberts take the lead with six laps left and win by a car length. It was the only Cup race the place ever held, and NASCAR was gone from the city for the next sixty-seven years.

name: Augusta International Raceway
body: Fireball Roberts designed a racetrack in Hephzibah, Georgia, then won the last race of his life on it. The Augusta 510 ran twenty-one turns through pine woods and spring-fed lakes in November 1963, and Roberts was dead the following summer of burns he took at Charlotte. Augusta International is a county park now and almost nobody walking it knows.

name: Piedmont Interstate Fairgrounds
body: Before Charlotte, the center of stock car racing was Spartanburg, South Carolina, and the half-mile dirt at the Piedmont Interstate Fairgrounds was the room where it happened. NASCAR's top series ran there twenty-two times between 1953 and 1966. Lee Petty won the first one. Ned Jarrett won six. Cotton Owens lived down the road and beat everybody at his own place. Then Charlotte Motor Speedway opened in 1960, the shops and the money followed it north, and by 1966 Spartanburg was just a town the sport used to live in.

name: Rambi Raceway
body: Rambi Raceway opened in 1958 on Highway 501 outside Myrtle Beach, a half-mile of dirt that got paved in 1974 and became Myrtle Beach Speedway. Cup ran there from 1958 through 1965. Every generation of Pettys took a green flag on that track, and so did three generations of Earnhardts. The land sold to a developer in 2020, the last flag fell that August, and by December 2021 most of the place was scraped off. Sixty-two years of racing, beaten by a survey stake.

name: Starkey Speedway
body: Starkey Speedway sat on 30 acres outside Roanoke, a quarter-mile with seats for 4,000 and a promoter who would book anything. Circus elephants one week, Grand National cars the next. Junior Johnson won the last NASCAR race there in August 1964 and took home $850, with Ned Jarrett second and Glen Wood third, three future Hall of Famers on one quarter-mile. The owners offered to spend half a million turning it into a half-mile if NASCAR would commit to two dates. NASCAR said no and went to the cities. There are soccer goals and ball diamonds on it now.

name: Speedway Park
body: Speedway Park was a half-mile of Jacksonville dirt with two turns, splintered wood grandstands and enough potholes to stop a race while somebody filled them. On December 1, 1963, Wendell Scott beat Buck Baker there and became the first Black driver to win a NASCAR Grand National race. They waved the flag at Baker first, then a scoring review found Scott had won it by two laps, and Scott went home that night without the trophy. The track closed in 1973 and there is an apartment complex on it now. Some ground deserves a marker.

name: Metrolina Speedway
body: Metrolina Speedway sat on the fairgrounds in northeast Charlotte, a half-mile of clay that ran Friday nights while Ralph Earnhardt and most of the Carolinas came to beat on each other. It got paved for a stretch in the 1970s to chase NASCAR money, and Dale Earnhardt won his first race on pavement there before the promoters gave up and put the dirt back. The gates are shut and a FedEx building sits next door, but the track is still out there, the last old Charlotte speedway left standing. Race City forgot one of its own.

name: Bryar Motorsports Park
body: Before the Magic Mile, Loudon was Bryar Motorsports Park, a 1.6-mile, ten-turn road course Keith Bryar finished in June 1965 on the site of a quarter-mile dirt oval called 106 Midway Raceway. It got by for twenty-five years on motorcycle weekends, and Bryar admitted the racing there made just barely enough to cover expenses. Bob Bahre bought it for $950,000 in December 1989, bulldozed it, and put a superspeedway where the road course used to run. Cup cars go back to that ground Sunday.

name: Southside Speedway
body: They called it the Toughest Short Track in the South, and for six decades Southside Speedway earned every word of it. The little bullring outside Richmond opened in 1959 and put Junior Johnson, Jim Paschal, and Ned Jarrett in Victory Lane during its Cup days, then spent forty more years turning local kids into racers, a young Denny Hamlin among them. It went dark in 2020 and sat silent. A revival group now has county approval and is working to fire the place back up. Some tracks are just too stubborn to stay dead.

name: Ontario Motor Speedway
body: They called it the Indianapolis of the West, and for one decade it might have been the most ambitious racetrack ever built in America. Ontario Motor Speedway opened outside Los Angeles in 1970 as the only facility on earth designed to host all four major sanctioning bodies, NASCAR, Indy cars, Formula 1, and the dragsters, all on one enormous complex. It hosted the Cup season finale through the 1970s, and in 1979 Richard Petty clinched his record seventh championship there by eleven points over Darrell Waltrip. Then the money ran out. By the end of 1980 the biggest, newest superspeedway in the country was sold off and bulldozed for a business park. It lasted ten years and left a hole nothing ever filled.

name: Daytona Beach and Road Course
body: Before there was a Daytona 500, there was the beach. The Daytona Beach and Road Course ran 4.1 miles half on the sand and half on old Highway A1A, and for years it was the wildest race on the schedule. Paul Goldsmith won the last one there in February 1958, leading all 39 laps and holding off Curtis Turner by five car lengths in front of 35,000 people. Bill France had already broken ground on his new superspeedway up the road, and once it opened the beach course had no reason left to exist. The track that helped build NASCAR simply went back to being a beach.

name: Islip Speedway
body: Islip Speedway was a fifth-mile of asphalt on Long Island, the smallest track NASCAR's Grand National division ever ran. Richard Petty won the last Cup race there in 1971, then NASCAR cut every race under 250 miles and never came back. The little joint also birthed the demolition derby in 1958 and put it on ABC's Wide World of Sports. The gates closed in 1984, and the bullring that punched way above its weight became just another Long Island memory.

name: Savannah Speedway
body: Savannah Speedway ran stock cars on the Georgia coast for two decades, a half-mile that opened as dirt in 1960, got paved, then went back to dirt at the very end. NASCAR's Grand National stars ran it ten times, and Richard Petty took three of them. One of the marquee dates was a St. Patrick's Day 200, because Savannah always did like a party. The pavement came up in 1981 and the gates closed that June, another coastal short track swallowed by time.

name: Trenton Speedway
body: Trenton Speedway was a mile and a half of oddball genius up in New Jersey, a kidney-bean oval with a 20-degree right-hand dogleg cut straight into the backstretch. Grand National came north eight times, and Richard Petty owned the place with three wins in the Northern 300. The gates closed in 1980, and today the old speedway grounds are a sculpture park. Not many tracks trade horsepower for bronze.

name: Middle Georgia Raceway
body: Middle Georgia Raceway in Byron ran NASCAR's Grand National stars from 1966 to 1971, and Richard Petty, Bobby Allison, David Pearson and Bobby Isaac all found victory lane on its half-mile. The wildest chapter came in 1967, when federal agents uncovered a full moonshine still hidden in a cave under turn three, reached by a trap door in a ticket booth and rigged to run 80 gallons a day. A track built on stock car racing, sitting right on top of the very thing that started it. The gates closed for good in the 1980s.

name: Lakewood Speedway
body: They called Lakewood Speedway the "Indianapolis of the South," a flat one-mile dirt oval carved around a lake at the Atlanta fairgrounds. Barney Oldfield and Ralph DePalma raced there in 1917, the NASCAR Grand National boys tore it up through the 1950s, and that murky infield pond swallowed more than one car that got loose in the corners. Atlanta International Raceway stole its thunder in 1960 and the gates finally closed in 1979. One of the great cathedrals of Southern racing, and most fans have never heard the name.

name: Charlotte Speedway
body: Before the 1.5-mile superspeedway, there was the original Charlotte Speedway, a rough three-quarter-mile dirt oval off Little Rock Road. It hosted the very first NASCAR Strictly Stock race on June 19, 1949, won by Jim Roper after the leader was disqualified for moonshiner's springs welded to his rear end. The track ran through 1956 and sits under an industrial park now, but Race City USA was born in that red dust.

name: Langhorne Speedway
body: Langhorne Speedway in Pennsylvania was one continuous mile of dirt with no straightaways, a giant circle they called the Big Left Turn. Curtis Turner won a race there in NASCAR's very first Strictly Stock season in 1949, and Fireball Roberts, Herb Thomas and the Flock brothers all wrestled its cursed "Puke Hollow." It was the most feared track in America, and the bulldozers took it for a shopping center in 1971. Some places you don't get back.

name: Columbia Speedway
body: Columbia Speedway in Cayce, South Carolina ran NASCAR's top division from 1951 to 1971, a half-mile of red clay they called the track too fast to handle. David Pearson, Buddy Baker, Junior Johnson and Fireball Roberts all turned laps in that dust. The Cup cars left in 1971 and the gates closed for good in 1975, but volunteers have since clawed the old oval back from the weeds. Some ghosts are worth keeping.

name: Asheville-Weaverville Speedway
body: Asheville-Weaverville Speedway started in 1950 as a half-mile dirt oval that a reformed bootlegger carved out of his own farm near Weaverville, NC. Lee Petty, Richard Petty, Rex White and Fireball Roberts all won there before the paved half-mile ran its last race in 1969 and closed for good in 1970. The land became a high school. Some of NASCAR's earliest proving ground now sits under classrooms and a parking lot.

name: Raleigh Speedway
body: Raleigh Speedway turned on the lights before anybody else. The one-mile oval hosted NASCAR's first superspeedway race under the lights in 1953 and ran its final three Grand National events on the Fourth of July, 1956 through 1958. Noise complaints from the neighbors shut it down, bulldozers finished the job in 1967, and a track that should be a shrine now sits mostly buried under the city. Some history deserved a better ending.

name: Riverside International Raceway
body: Riverside International Raceway ran from 1957 to 1989 in the California desert east of Los Angeles, a twisting road course that tested NASCAR, Formula 1, and sports cars on the same asphalt. When the land got worth more than the racing, the bulldozers won and the property became a shopping mall. A track that humbled the best now sells sneakers where the esses used to be.

name: Occoneechee Speedway
body: Before Talladega, before Daytona got fast, there was a one-mile dirt oval carved out of an old horse farm in Hillsborough, North Carolina. Occoneechee Speedway ran from 1948 to 1968, one of just two tracks from NASCAR's inaugural 1949 season, and the only dirt track from that first year still standing today. Junior Johnson and Curtis Turner slid through those corners, Richard Petty took the final checkered there in 1968, and now it's a quiet wooded trail you can walk.
